clue.text: Press editor upset about daily's central spread

indicators.note: about says the rearranged letters go round the single letter picked next
upset means overturned or disturbed, so the letters before it are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: central picks the middle letter of the word daily

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor is annoyed about the centre pages of a daily paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' makes DSPERSE, and 'about' wraps that round the 'central' letter. 'spread' reads as a newspaper's centre pages but is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To spread things is to scatter them over a wide area, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Will unprepared goes around river road in us

indicators.note: goes around says the word for having no will encloses the abbreviation that follows

parts.note: someone who dies with no will prepared is said to be intestate
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A man called Will, not ready, drives round a riverside road in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like a man's name at the start of the sentence; it is the legal document, and 'goes around' wraps the word for lacking one round the river.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: the major highways crossing state lines in America are called interstates.

clue.text: Officer in charge blocks European artist

indicators.note: blocks means sits in the way inside, so the abbreviation is lodged within the word for a European

parts.note: a Pole is a person from Poland, so a European
John Constable was the English landscape painter of The Hay Wain

explanation.surface: An officer who is in command stands in the way of a painter from the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in charge' reads as describing the officer; it is the abbreviation IC, which 'blocks' puts inside the European.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: this is the lowest rank of British police, the ordinary bobby on the beat.

clue.text: What restaurant serving steak tartare shouldn't offer?

definitions.text: What restaurant serving steak tartare shouldn't offer?

parts.words: What restaurant serving steak tartare shouldn't offer?
parts.note: steak tartare is uncooked minced beef, so the place literally deals in uncooked food; the phrase wanted is the idiom for unfair treatment, which no customer should get

explanation.surface: A question about what a restaurant with steak tartare on the menu ought not to serve.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for unfair treatment, punning on the uncooked beef such a kitchen hands out.

clue.text: Get the measure of an 'orrible place

definitions.meaning: an old unit of length for cloth, about 45 inches in England
the horrible place is hell, and a speaker who says 'orrible drops that aitch as well

explanation.surface: Someone sizes up a dreadful spot, speaking in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get the measure of' reads as the idiom for sizing something up; only 'measure' defines. The dropped aitch of 'orrible shows how the speaker would say the name of the horrible place.
explanation.definitionFit: An old cloth-measuring unit of about 45 inches, and the underworld as an aitch-dropping Londoner would pronounce it.

clue.text: Simple soldier initially in corps facing intense dislike

indicators.note: facing says the abbreviation for corps stands directly in front of the word for dislike

parts.note: C is an abbreviation for corps, as in the initials of army units

indicators.note: in puts the soldier's opening letter inside the two pieces that follow it

parts.note: hate is intense dislike

indicators.note: initially takes only the opening letter of soldier

explanation.surface: A naive private, new to his army corps, meets fierce hostility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes S from soldier and 'in' puts it inside C and HATE, which 'facing' sets side by side. 'Simple' reads as naive but means plain in style.
explanation.definitionFit: Said of style or design, it means plain and unadorned, a synonym in that restrained sense.

clue.text: Cautious about books in place for sung mass

indicators.note: about says the word for cautious goes round the abbreviation for books

parts.note: chary means wary or cautious
NT is the New Testament, a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone is wary about the hymn books left where a choral service is held.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapel endowed so that priests would sing masses for the founder's soul.

clue.text: Description of an eel taken from okeechobee lake

definitions.text: Description of an eel taken from okeechobee lake

parts.words: Description of an eel taken from okeechobee lake
parts.note: an eel lifted from a Florida lake is a swimming creature removed from its element, which is the idiom for someone ill at ease; the letters e, e, l also run across the end of okeechobee and the start of lake

explanation.surface: Someone describes an eel caught in Florida's Lake Okeechobee.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'eel' run across the end of 'okeechobee' and the start of 'lake', so the eel is literally 'taken from' the lake's name as well as from the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for someone out of their element, which is literally the state of an eel lifted from a lake.

clue.text: What's changed in period of warmer weather?

indicators.note: changed says the letters of the word before it are put in a new order

parts.note: the letters used are those of the word what; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is different during a mild spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's' looks like the start of a question; 'changed' rearranges the four letters of WHAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A spell when temperatures rise and the ice and snow melt.

clue.text: Empty viscount's not entirely antique type of aircraft

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its inside, leaving only the first and last letters of viscount
not entirely means the word for antique is used without its final letter

parts.note: antique as an adjective means old

explanation.surface: A vacuous nobleman owns a kind of plane that is not quite a museum piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' leaves VT from viscount and 'not entirely' trims OLD to OL. The answer is an acronym, vertical take-off and landing.
explanation.definitionFit: An acronym for vertical take-off and landing, the class of plane that includes the Harrier jump jet.

clue.text: Harry and William in a jaguar perhaps

indicators.note: to harry is to harass or ravage, so the words after it are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written: it is part of the fodder, not a joining word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Princes Harry and William ride in a Jaguar car, or something like it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like the prince beside his brother; it is a verb, and it rearranges AND plus WILLIAM. The Jaguar of the surface is a British make of car.
explanation.definitionFit: The big cat of the Americas is one example of an untamed creature, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: In which you could see MCC hat-trick bagging Yorkshire's tail

definitions.text: In which you could see MCC hat-trick bagging Yorkshire's tail

indicators.note: bagging means catching or taking in, so the rearranged letters hold the single letter picked next
you could see these letters differently: the phrase invites viewing them in another arrangement

parts.note: taken as written; MCC is the Marylebone club based at Lord's in London
taken as written, without the hyphen

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its last letter, here that of Yorkshire

explanation.surface: An MCC bowler takes three wickets in three balls to finish off the last Yorkshire batsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could see' makes CRICKTMATCH, which 'bagging' opens for the 'tail' letter. The whole clue also defines: a hat-trick is three wickets in successive balls, the tail a side's weakest batsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: A game between the Marylebone club and a county is where three wickets in successive balls could remove the last batsmen.

clue.text: Mother runs around mostly for the stork!

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: mostly means the word for around is used without its last letter

parts.note: around and about are synonyms

explanation.surface: An expectant mother dashes about getting ready for the stork's delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims ABOUT to ABOU. The surface plays on the stork that brings babies.
explanation.definitionFit: A large African bird of that family, so a specific kind of the bird named.

clue.text: Tip denied baseball official

parts.note: to deny a request is to refuse it
ump is the short form of umpire, the official who rules on play in baseball

explanation.surface: A baseball umpire is not given a gratuity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like a gratuity; here it is the British word for a rubbish dump.
explanation.definitionFit: In British English a tip is the site where household rubbish is taken and left.

clue.text: Put the French right? I may do that precisely

parts.note: to stick something somewhere is an informal way of saying put it there
le is the French word for the

explanation.surface: A pedant boasts of being the one to correct the French exactly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' points back to the first half: putting people right is what this person does, so the wordplay words also colour the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedant who insists on exactness is the person likely to correct others with precision.

clue.text: True statement to a gambler certainly

definitions.meaning: said to a gambler, the two words are a plain fact: that person does place wagers
an informal, emphatic way of saying yes

explanation.surface: A punter is told something reliable, for sure.
explanation.definitionFit: Addressed to a punter the phrase is a literal fact about wagering, and colloquially it is an emphatic yes.

clue.text: Number in groups backed lots of rock

indicators.note: backed means the whole assembled string is read from right to left
in places the abbreviation for number inside the word for groups

parts.note: sets are groups of things that belong together

explanation.surface: A song among bands gave support to a great deal of rock music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' makes SENOTS, which 'backed' then turns round whole. 'Number' and 'rock' suggest music; the rock is the mineral kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumps of mineral matter: a pile of them is a quantity of rock.

clue.text: Rush around place for a binge

indicators.note: around says the word for rush encloses the abbreviation for place

parts.note: a surge is a sudden rush forward
Pl is the abbreviation for place in street names

explanation.surface: People hurry about a venue to get to a drinking session.
explanation.definitionFit: A bout of extravagant spending or indulgence, a synonym for a spree.

clue.text: Keep quiet, British f1 driver's in court

parts.note: Jenson Button is a British Formula One driver, world champion in 2009
someone up before a judge is appearing in court

explanation.surface: Hush: a British racing driver is appearing before a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial order to stop talking, as in fastening one's lip.

clue.text: No 1 position whichever way you look at it

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: looking from either direction gives the same letters, the mark of a phrase that reads identically forwards and backwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Someone is ranked first no matter how the results are viewed.
explanation.definitionFit: First place in a ranking or chart is its highest slot.

clue.text: A fine mineral improved world cup team

indicators.note: improved means altered for the better, so the three words after it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, twelve letters

explanation.surface: A good mineral supplement made a World Cup squad better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine' reads as good; it means finely ground. 'improved' rearranges WORLD CUP TEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft mineral ground to a very fine dust for use on the skin.

clue.text: Right and wrong stitch

indicators.note: wrong, placed after the fodder, says its letters are out of their proper order

parts.note: taken as written: it is part of the fodder, not a joining word

explanation.surface: A stitch can be done correctly or incorrectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is not a link here: it joins R as the letters that 'wrong' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to mend a hole in fabric with interwoven threads, so to sew.

clue.text: Style of male singing at the cutting edge?

definitions.text: Style of male singing at the cutting edge?

parts.words: Style of male singing at the cutting edge?
parts.note: close-harmony quartets of men are named after the place where blades trim hair, which is the literal cutting edge

explanation.surface: A kind of men's vocal music that is thoroughly avant-garde.
explanation.definitionFit: Close-harmony quartets of men take their name from the place where hair is trimmed.

clue.text: Cool fruit and it can nowadays be replaced

definitions.meaning: fashionably up to date, in informal speech
the red berry of the wild rose
the joint at the top of the thigh, routinely swapped for an artificial one in modern surgery

explanation.surface: Chilled fruit, and something that modern life lets you swap.
explanation.definitionFit: Fashionable in slang, the rose's red berry, and the thigh joint that surgeons now routinely renew.

clue.text: Go round singular French city

indicators.note: the city's name looks like a plural, so making it singular drops its plural ending

parts.note: Tours is a city on the Loire in central France

explanation.surface: Someone takes a trip around a remarkable French city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singular' reads as remarkable; it tells you to treat TOURS as a plural and take off its S.
explanation.definitionFit: To travel around a place visiting its sights.

clue.text: Stick and where you should put it

definitions.meaning: to cling or be fixed within something, as a quality belongs to a thing
split into two words, it is what someone says while pointing at the spot before them

explanation.surface: A stick, and advice on where to stow it.
explanation.definitionFit: As one word it means to be fixed or rooted within something; split in two it points to this very spot.

clue.text: Underground support for power in points? Not on

indicators.note: in places the two short pieces inside what is left of the word points
Not tells you the letters of the word after it are to be taken out of points

parts.note: taken as written before the removal
taken as written, its two letters removed separately
pro means in favour of, or for
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: Backing below ground for electrical power at the railway points? It has been called off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on' removes two letters that are not adjacent, leaving PITS, before 'in' applies. The surface's railway switches and electricity are only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber posts that hold up the roof of a mine, so props used below ground.
